title: Morgan County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Morgan County wells have a 91-foot median depth. Compare reported yields, water levels and estimated finished-well costs of $9,200-$17,000.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Morgan County
intro_html:
A shallow well is not automatically a simple well project. Morgan County's median recorded depth is 91 feet, but legal water use, aquifer conditions and the cost of getting water to the house matter just as much as footage.

Colorado DWR records include 9,706 permits countywide, with 6,454 wells recorded as constructed. These records cover household, stock, irrigation and monitoring uses—not just rural homes. Use the county figures to start a budget, then check nearby wells around Fort Morgan, Brush, Wiggins or the specific area where you plan to buy.

sections.heading: A 91-Foot Median, With Local Ground Doing the Deciding
sections.html:
Among 6,990 wells reporting depth, the median is 91 feet and the middle half falls between 62 and 126 feet. That makes relatively shallow drilling a reasonable starting assumption, but a bid should still allow for the actual formation encountered. The 90th-percentile depth is 170 feet; the deepest record reaches 1,625 feet and is not a typical household benchmark.

Morgan County's drilling ground includes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name Quaternary Alluvium for 571 wells and Alluvial for 438. The large unnamed / fractured-bedrock category is not proof that a particular lot sits over fractured rock. Compare nearby completion logs around Weldona, Orchard or Hillrose before selecting a target depth.

sections.heading: Strong Reported Yields, but Not All From Household Wells
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 20 gpm, with the middle half spanning 15-900 gpm. That unusually wide range needs context: irrigation accounts for 27% of recorded uses, stock for 25%, and domestic/household for 38%. A large irrigation-well result is not a sensible promise for a new house well.

Of the 1,910 wells reporting yield, 88% fall in the 15+ gpm category and 2% in the 1-5 gpm category. The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, but that does not establish that unsuccessful drilling never occurs. For a purchase, get a current sustained pumping test and recovery assessment. A permit's reported output is neither a current performance guarantee nor permission to pump that amount for any use.

sections.heading: Water Below Ground Is Not the Same as Drilling Depth
sections.html:
Static water level is where water stands in a resting well, not the bottom of the hole. Morgan County's median is 33 feet below ground, with the middle half at 17-60 feet. Only 407 records report this measurement, so it is a much smaller sample than the depth records.

The decade medians do not show a steady countywide decline. Depth to water increased from 35 feet in the 1950s to 50 feet in the 1970s, then became shallower, reaching 20 feet in the 2000s. It was 21 feet in the 2010s and 37 feet in the 2020s. That recent deeper reading deserves attention, but these are different groups of measurements—not repeat monitoring of the same wells. Check local history and pumping drawdown before drawing conclusions about your parcel.

sections.heading: Morgan County's Drilling Record Runs Through 2025
sections.html:
Permit activity spans decades: 1,069 permits were issued in the 1970s, 1,044 in the 2000s, 723 in the 2010s and 440 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so the latest decade is incomplete and should not be compared as a full period. Permit issuance also does not mean every authorized well was built.

The most frequent named driller entries are Canfield Drilling Company (Canfield, Harold E), with 1,242 records, and Canfield, Leslie George, with 934. Another 563 entries read Authorized (Pe, Pg), which is not a specific drilling-company name. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. For an existing well near Snyder or Log Lane Village, the original construction report can be more useful than the permit date alone.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Hole in Morgan County
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 91-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $3,200-$5,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $9,200-$17,000.

Treat those as planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote. The 62-126-foot middle depth range means a driller needs nearby logs and a clear scope before committing to footage. Ask the bid to spell out casing, grout, development, testing and what happens if more depth is required. Also confirm the assumed trench route and electrical connection. On a rural lot outside Brush or Wiggins, getting water from the well to the building can be a substantial part of the work.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Leave Room for Septic
sections.html:
The environmental map lists 35 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular Morgan County well is contaminated. Review the individual site's status and groundwater setting, then ask a qualified laboratory or local health authority which tests fit the property. A clear-looking sample is not a safety determination.

Inspect the wellhead, casing condition, grout documentation and drainage around the well. For a building lot, lay out the well, septic system, replacement septic area, house and access together before drilling. Keep the drilling location accessible for future service. Strong countywide yield reports cannot eliminate a low-yield or unsuccessful hole on an individual parcel; discuss that possibility in the drilling contract.

sections.heading: Before Closing on Land Near Fort Morgan or Wiggins
sections.html:
Start with the actual parcel and its DWR permit, not the listing's description of a “domestic well.” Confirm the authorized uses and any restrictions on outdoor watering or livestock. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize irrigation. Depending on the water source and proposed use, an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

For an existing home, obtain the completion report, pump records, current water-quality results and a pumping test. For vacant land around Morgan Heights, Trail Side or Saddle Ridge, compare nearby wells by location, aquifer and use rather than relying on the county median alone. Have the driller and site contractor review access, septic placement and utility routing before you settle the house location or treat the well allowance as final.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Morgan County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth in Morgan County is 91 feet, and the middle half is 62-126 feet. Those figures come from 6,990 records reporting depth. Local alluvium and sedimentary formations affect the target, so nearby construction logs are a better guide for a particular lot than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Morgan County?
faq.a: The planning rate is $35-$55 per foot. At the county's 91-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,200-$5,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $9,200-$17,000. Ask for a written scope that addresses casing, grout, testing, additional depth and the utility route to the house.

faq.q: How much water do Morgan County wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 20 gpm, and 88% of reporting wells are in the 15+ gpm category. These records include irrigation and stock wells as well as household wells. Before buying, use a sustained pumping test to check current output and recovery, and verify that the permit allows your intended use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Morgan County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through testing and inspection. The area map includes 35 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not establish contamination. Review nearby site details and get laboratory testing suited to the property's groundwater risks.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Morgan County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not establish a steady countywide decline. Median depth to water was 50 feet in the 1970s, 20 feet in the 2000s and 37 feet in the 2020s. The recent deeper reading warrants a local check, but the records are not repeated measurements from a fixed set of wells.
